refuted.telling_ending: The advisors suggested different methods to educate the princes, but one advisor, Keen, had a clever idea. He said, "Your Majesty, we can't teach them in a short time. They need to learn the basics of grammar, then move on to books on religion and practical life. It will take twelve years."
refuted.source_resolution: corpus/stories/PT002-introduction.txt is a clean, complete chapter (74 lines, no hand-off). Line 40: "And they, one after another, replied: 'O King, first one learns grammar, in twelve years...'" — the twelve-year curriculum belongs to the counselors collectively. Line 42 then singles out Keen with the OPPOSITE proposal: "But one of their number, a counselor named Keen, said: 'O King, the duration of life is limited... Therefore let some kind of epitome be devised to wake their intelligence.'"
refuted.discrepancy: The telling places the counselors' twelve-year doctrine in KEEN's mouth as his "clever idea" (line 9), then has Keen give the epitome idea as "another idea" (line 11). Source assigns "twelve years" to the advisors en masse and reserves Keen for the epitome proposal — Keen's whole rhetorical role is to reject the long-timeline view. The telling thereby inverts who holds which position. The parallel 4-9 band gets this right ("The advisors said, 'Learning takes a long time. It takes twelve years...' One advisor, Keen, said, 'Learning is hard. It takes too long...'"), which shows the 9+ band's compression is a genuine attribution slip, not a stylistic choice.

refuted.telling_ending: Lively became exhausted and sank in the mud. The driver reported to Increase that Lively had died.

In killing him, I have only hurt myself"). For the driver point specifically: source line 806 — the driver tells the merchant only "Lively was wearied by the trip, and sank in the mud"; the FALSE death report is made later by the OTHER MEN at line 810: "the men, fearing the many drawbacks of the forest... made a false report to their master. 'Poor Lively died,' they said."
refuted.discrepancy: The telling gives the false death report to the DRIVER (line 5: "The driver reported to Increase that Lively had died"). The source gives the driver a truthful mud-report and assigns the death-lie to "the men" (line 810). This also makes the telling internally incoherent: Increase is told Lively died, yet immediately "left caretakers with Lively's food and said, 'If he lives, bring him to me; if he dies, perform the last rites'" (line 7). The 4-9 band keeps the two reports separate and correct, so this is a 9+-only slip. (Line 7 of the same telling does also credit "the men" with the false report, so it is a duplicated/contradictory attribution rather than a clean reassignment — but line 5's driver-death claim diverges from source line 806.)

refuted.telling_ending: The jackal laughed and said, "I was so silly! I thought it was full of food!" / Moral: Don't judge something by its noise or appearance.

Source line 10: "Now when the drum was struck by the tips of grasses swaying in the wind, it made the sound, but was dumb at other times." The source has the drum sounding WHILE the wind blows (the swaying grass strikes it) and silent otherwise; the telling says it was quiet while the wind blew. The 9+ sibling renders it correctly, confirming this is a 4-9-only error, not my misreading.

refuted.telling_ending: The next day, Bull entered the palace and made another false accusation against the king. The king realized his mistake and reinstated Strong-Tooth, presenting him with gems and garments. Moral: A little thing can lift someone high, and a little thing can bring them down.

Source line 156: "Now Bull received the two garments as if they were the Kingdom of Heaven, and feeling intense satisfaction, he said: 'Friend merchant, I forgive you.'" The source casts Bull - the actual wrongdoer - as the magnanimous party who FORGIVES Strong-Tooth; nobody apologizes. The telling flips this: Bull is now the contrite party who apologizes. The relationship is reversed.

refuted.telling_ending: Bull, the king's lowly servant, was jealous of Strong-Tooth's position. He thought, "Why should I be angry? I won't hurt him. I'll just wait for the right moment." ... Strong-Tooth ... explaining that he had driven him out because of his misbehavior.

So Strong-Tooth administered a cuffing and drove him out. From that moment the humiliation so rankled in Bull's inner soul that he had no rest even at night."
refuted.discrepancy: The telling invents Bull's motive as jealousy of Strong-Tooth's position and silently drops the source's actual cause of the grudge: Bull usurped a seat before the king's professor and was cuffed and driven out by Strong-Tooth. The telling's later line ("he had driven him out because of his misbehavior") has no referent in the telling because the cuffing/wrong-seat incident was never shown - it survives only in the source. (Minor, same paragraph: the telling adds that Bull "saw Strong-Tooth near the king's bed," whereas in the source Bull was sweeping near the KING's bed and fabricated the queen accusation without sighting Strong-Tooth.)

refuted.telling_ending: At the river, Godly gave June his robe to watch. June took the treasure and ran away. Moral: Trusting no one can lead to trouble.

The following material (the ram-fight / jackal spectacle, complete.txt line 2227) is a NEW nested tale, not this fable's resolution - so the telling is NOT truncated and correctly stops at the decampment.

The body shows Godly "trusted no one with his treasure" and kept it under his arm, yet he is still robbed; the only act of trust the body depicts - Godly handing June his robe to watch - is exactly what causes the loss. No depicted event shows distrust causing trouble; the tale actually dramatizes distrust FAILING to prevent it. The moral is unsupported (arguably inverted) by the telling's own body, which alone carries the moral since the 9+ sibling has none.

refuted.telling_ending: As soon as Godly was out of sight, June seized the treasure and ran away.
refuted.source_resolution: corpus/stories/PT007-godly-and-june.txt:94 "Still, Godly kept his treasure under his arm." and :96, June's own words: "Do what I will, he does not trust me." — the distrust runs FROM Godly TO June.
refuted.discrepancy: Telling line 13 reads: "As time passed, June served Godly, but still didn't trust him." Read plainly, the subject 'June' carries through, so the sentence has JUNE distrusting Godly — the reverse of the source, where it is Godly who does not trust June (:94, :96). The following clause ("He thought of killing Godly") confirms 'He' = June. The source's actual engine — Godly hoarding the treasure because he does not trust his disciple — is thus reassigned to June. Caveat for the reviewer: the pronoun is ambiguous, and if 'him' is read with a subject switch ('[Godly] still didn't trust him [June]') the sense matches the source, so this may be merely loose phrasing rather than a slip; flagged under the default-to-flag-when-uncertain rule.

refuted.telling_ending: creep.txt:9 -- She agreed to let Leap stay, but with a condition: "You must not bite the king when he's drunk, tired, or asleep. That's the right time and place." The body then ends correctly: the servants "found Creep and her family, killing them instead" (line 11), Leap hides and escapes (line 13).
refuted.source_resolution: corpus/stories/PT015-leap-and-creep.txt line 44: "When the king's body is mastered by wine, fatigue, or sleep, then you may quietly bite him on the feet. This is the right place and the right time." The fable's resolution is at line 48 (Creep and her family killed). The source has Leap err by biting the WRONG PLACE (back, not feet) at roughly the sanctioned time; the telling makes the safe time itself forbidden. Note: the telling's own trailing clause ("That's the right time and place") signals the writer meant the source's meaning, so this reads as a literal negation slip -- but as written the deal is inverted and a reader would take away the wrong rule.

refuted.telling_ending: Telling (corpus/age/9+/PT018-ugly-s-trust-abused.txt L15): "Haughty, moved by Ugly's words, gave the order, and the others tore Ugly's body apart. They devoured him, and Ugly finally gave up the ghost." Ending itself matches source.
refuted.source_resolution: corpus/stories/PT018-ugly-s-trust-abused.txt L149: "Hereupon the lion gave the word, the leopard and the jackal tore his body, the crow pecked out his eyes, poor Ugly yielded up the ghost, and all the others ravenously devoured him."
refuted.discrepancy: The telling reverses the mechanism of the food crisis (L7): "However, Haughty soon fell ill and couldn't hunt for food. His companions, the leopard, the crow, and the jackal, grew tired and hungry. They begged Haughty to let them find food for him, but he refused, saying he was on a diet." Source L12 gives a different cause: "the lion fought an elephant one day, received a thrust from a tusk, and had to keep his cave" -- not illness. More importantly the INITIATIVE is inverted: in the source the LION repeatedly orders his followers to hunt (L14-16: "You will just have to make an effort on your own account." / "Round up some food-animal for me while I am in this condition." / "Come! Do not be bashful. Hunt up some creature."), while they demur ("Why should we care to thrive, while our lord and king is in this state?"); the telling has the companions begging to hunt and the lion REFUSING. Also the phrase "on a diet" is the JACKAL's about the lion in the source (corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt L4442, L4456: "the king is on a diet"), not the lion's own refusal. Downstream beats (jackal's proposal, Ugly volunteering to outdo the others, the kill) are accurate; only this framing line contradicts the source.

refuted.telling_ending: Line 10: Shell-Neck said, "Please don't go. I will die here. You can fly away, but I will drown." (The telling then ends correctly: line 24 'He lost his grip and fell. People cut him up with knives.' + Moral.)

(panchatantra_complete.txt line 4790)

The 4-9 telling makes Shell-Neck say 'I will drown' -- death by excess water -- the opposite mechanism, impossible in a dried-up lake. The 9+ telling states it correctly ('die quickly from thirst'), so this is unique to the 4-9 telling. The census marked this RESOLVES with 'discrepancy: None' because it compared only the final events; the contradiction is in the body dialogue, not the ending.

refuted.telling_ending: corpus/age/9+/PT026-smart-the-jackal.txt line 13: "The lion fled, leaving Smart to eat the camel's body. Smart ate the meat slowly, making it last a long time." Then line 15: "Moral: Those who use their intelligence to harm others will eventually be punished for their selfish deeds."

refuted.telling_ending: corpus/age/9+/PT026-smart-the-jackal.txt line 11: "Meat-Face blamed Smart, but the lion realized he was innocent."

But Smart laughed and said: 'Come, come! You ate the camel's heart all by yourself. Why do you look at me?'" -- it is SMART who accuses Meat-Face. Meat-Face then flees (line 35, "fled for his life") and the lion pursues briefly before turning back ("He, too, it is unguipugnacious. I must not kill him.").

The source has Smart frame Meat-Face (the guilty party deflects onto his accomplice); the telling has Meat-Face blaming Smart, casting Smart as the accused. The telling also invents a beat -- "the lion realized he was innocent" -- that replaces the source's roar ("Who turned this camel into leavings? I wish to kill him, too.") and drops Meat-Face's flight and the lion's turn-back entirely.

refuted.telling_ending: Right-Mind said, "Please come out, goddess." / The voice did not come out. / So the magistrates looked inside the tree. / They found Wrong-Mind's father hiding there. / The trick was exposed. / Wrong-Mind had to give back the stolen money. / Right-Mind was free.
refuted.source_resolution: corpus/stories/PT031-*.txt ends on the hand-off at line 66 ("How was that?" asked Wrong-Mind. And his father told the story of). The fable's own resolution is in corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt:5826-5830: the father speaks from the tree (5826, "Gentlemen, Right-Mind took that money"); then (5828) "Meanwhile Right-Mind heaped inflammable matter about the hole in the mimosa and set fire to it. As the mimosa burned, Wrong-Mind's father issued from the hole with a pitiful wail, his body scorched and his eyes popping out"; (5830) "'It is all Wrong-Mind's doing,' he replied. Whereupon the king's men hanged Wrong-Mind to a branch of the mimosa, while they commended Right-Mind and caused him satisfaction by conferring upon him the king's favor and other things."
refuted.discrepancy: The telling invents the exposure mechanism. In the telling, Right-Mind verbally summons the goddess ("Please come out, goddess"), the voice refuses, and then "the magistrates looked inside the tree" and "found Wrong-Mind's father hiding there." None of this is in the source: the trick is exposed by Right-Mind SETTING FIRE to the mimosa (complete.txt:5828), which drives the scorched father out to confess (5830). The magistrates never search the tree, and Right-Mind never asks the goddess to come out. The census's stated reason for RESOLVES -- "the discovery in the tree is faithful" -- is factually wrong: the discovery is a fabricated substitution (a search) for the source's fire. The ending also changes the source outcome: Wrong-Mind merely returns the money and is "free" instead of being hanged. (The softened outcome alone could be defended as content-softening for age 4-9, but the fabricated discovery mechanism cannot -- the source's causal chain is replaced.)

refuted.telling_ending:
"The magistrates laughed and asked Naduk to explain. He told them the story of the balance-beam, and they laughed too. They ordered the balance-beam and Money-God to be returned to their rightful owners.

Moral: People often lie to cover up their own mistakes, but honesty is always the best policy."
refuted.source_resolution: The fable resolves IN-chapter, so the census's RESOLVES is right on resolution: stories/PT033-the-mice-that-ate-iron.txt line 64 (= panchatantra_complete.txt:6006) — '"How was that?" they asked, and Naduk told them the story of the balance-beam. At this they laughed and caused the restoration of balance-beam and boy to the respective owners.' The file's closing hand-off (stories line 156 'And Cheek told the story of') is the outer frame; the continuation at complete.txt:6098-6100 is a NEW nested tale, THE RESULTS OF EDUCATION (= PT034), NOT this fable's ending. So no truncation — but the source's own stated lesson for this fable is the retort verse at line 54/6047-6052: 'Where mice eat balance-beams of iron / A thousand pals in weight, / A hawk might steal an elephant; / A boy is trifling freight.' — a lesson about the clever counter-thrust, not honesty.
refuted.discrepancy: The Moral names an outcome the body never depicts and in fact inverts. Every load-bearing act is a lie: Lakshman lies ('Mice ate the balance-beam'), and Naduk wins by a fabrication he never retracts — 'A hawk carried him off' (telling lines 13, 19; source lines 48-50). Nobody is honest and no honest act is rewarded; the magistrates restore beam and boy because they laugh at Naduk's cheek (telling line 21: 'they laughed too'), which is the opposite of 'honesty is always the best policy'. The body supports at most 'a cheat is cheated'; the Moral asserts honesty pays. Source's lesson for this fable ('a hawk might steal an elephant; a boy is trifling freight') is likewise not about honesty, so the Moral is a softened/invented overlay (brief rule 7, 'do not soften the point'). Judgment call, stated honestly: the project's own tag endorses an 'honesty' frame (story_tags.json PT033 moral.text 'Honesty is always the best choice.', rationale 'honesty-vs-cunning is a real dilemma'), so a reviewer may read the Moral as intentionally ironic; but against the telling's own body it is unearned.

refuted.telling_ending:
Together, the doves managed to lift the snare and fly away, leaving the hunter frustrated.

Swift was impressed by Gay-Neck's leadership and teamwork skills. He realized that when friends work together, they can overcome even the most difficult challenges.

Moral: United action and teamwork can help overcome even the most daunting obstacles.
refuted.source_resolution: The PT037 chapter (corpus/stories/PT037-the-winning-of-friends.txt) ends on the hand-off at line 94: '"How was that?" asked the doves. And Gay-Neck told the story of'. The doves' own resolution is the continuation after the nested Bharunda tale: complete.txt 6553 'they united their efforts to carry the snare away, flew just an arrow-shot into the air' (they are STILL caught in the snare), the hunter pursues and gives up (6568), and finally 6720: 'After making these observations, Gold cut the bonds of all, then said to Gay-Neck: "Now, my friend, you are free to go home." So Gay-Neck went home with his retinue.'
refuted.discrepancy: The telling stops at the source's mid-beat. In the source the doves are still bound inside the snare when they fly off (they 'carry the snare away'); they are only freed when the mouse Gold cuts the bonds (6720). The telling never reaches that resolution — it ends with the doves flying off still in the snare and calls it done. The census excused this ('it ends on a genuine source consequence, not a plan or hand-off'), but the escape beat is not the resolution of the snare plot; the freeing by Gold is, and it is absent. The continuation is not a new nested tale (the Bharunda nested tale is a separate step and the doves' freeing follows it), so this is not the PT039 false-positive pattern.

refuted.telling_ending:
However, when the chief examined the thief's stomach, he found no gem.

Realizing his mistake, the chief released the travelers, and they continued their journey. The thief's selfless act saved his friends' lives, and they all reached a safe destination.

Moral: A sensible enemy can be a better friend than a selfish ally.
refuted.source_resolution: complete.txt 6178: 'To this the chief mercifully agreed, but he found no sign of a gem in the stomach, cut as he would... The three were therefore set free uninjured, and hastening through the forest, they reached a civilized spot.' Followed at 6182 by the source's own verse: 'The robber for his victims died.'
refuted.discrepancy: In the source the chief cuts the thief's stomach open and the thief DIES — only 'the three' are freed, and the source's moral verse is literally 'The robber for his victims died.' The telling softens 'cut as he would' to 'examined the thief's stomach,' then releases 'the travelers' and says 'they all reached a safe destination' — i.e. the thief, described earlier as a fellow traveller who 'joined their group,' survives. The death that the source's own moral turns on is removed, so the ending states the opposite outcome (all survive vs the thief dies).

refuted.source_resolution: corpus/stories/PT036-the-foolish-friend.txt line 6: 'he appointed the son of the man of learning his prime minister, planned to seize the kingdom of the monarch of that country, and made the merchant's son his secretary of the treasury.' The 4-9 telling says his greed 'made him eat too quickly', inverting the source's depicted behaviour and replacing its causal mechanism with a fast-eating death. refuted.telling_ending: The mice were sad and scared. They had a meeting. "We must help the elephants," they said. ... He remembered the mice who helped him.
refuted.source_resolution: corpus/stories/PT045-the-mice-that-set-elephants-free.txt:10 'We are being killed,' they said, 'by these lumbering elephants'; :22 the mice ask the elephant-king 'pray travel another path'; :28 the elephant-king reflects 'We have no means of deliverance except those mice'; :32 the mice 'set their friends free'.
refuted.discrepancy: The telling invents a motive the source does not contain: the mice convene and decide 'We must help the elephants' (line 15). In the source the convention is for the mice's OWN survival — they devise a remedy for their own crisis and beg the elephants to go another way (source ll.10,20-22). The telling also asserts the trapped king 'remembered the mice who helped him' (line 25), i.e. that the mice had previously done him a favor; the source's elephant recalls them only as his last hope ('We have no means of deliverance except those mice'), after HE had earlier granted THEM a favor. The reciprocal direction is inverted/imported. Confirming this is a genuine 4-9 slip and not an artifact: the sibling 9+ telling of the same fable renders the beat correctly ('We need a plan to stop them'; 'I have no way to escape except with the help of those clever mice').

The telling even self-contradicts: line 13 calls Slow 'the turtle' and has 'Swift would peck out my eyes' (bird action) while line 11 just called both 'deer'.

refuted.discrepancy: Line 29 'Gold, the deer, came up with a plan to save him.' Gold is the source's MOUSE, not a deer (source line 264 'The deer and turtle, mouse and crow'; Gold cuts the bonds and slips into a chink/grass-clump, lines 248-250). refuted.telling_ending: "He begged the Moon to forgive him and promised never to return. Then he went back to his own place, and the elephants never troubled the rabbits again. / Moral: Pretending to be something you're not can lead to trouble, and honesty is always the best policy."
refuted.source_resolution: Victory, a rabbit, poses as an envoy of the blessèd Moon; the elephant-king Four-Tusk, convinced he has sinned against the Moon, bows to the earth, promises "I shall never return here," and departs. The deception succeeds completely and the rabbits are left in peace.

notes:
Method: read each telling in full; read the source chapter; where the chapter ends on a hand-off, grep'd corpus/panchatantra_complete.txt for the continuation resolution.

TRUNCATION TRAP (both PT003 bands): corpus/stories/PT003-the-loss-of-friends.txt IS a hand-off chapter — it ends at line 106 "And Cheek told the story of" (start of PT004, the wedge-monkey tale). The real frame resolution is the continuation at complete.txt line 6267: "when Rusty had killed Lively, his wrath subsided into pity... 'Lively was almost my second life. In killing him, I have only hurt myself.'" Both tellings reach exactly that beat, so NEITHER is truncated and NEITHER is "invented" for showing the killing (the killing is the source's own continuation resolution, not fabrication). NB: Book I keeps going past 6267 only with Cheek's long sermon rebuking Victor and praising wise counsel (complete.txt 6340-6418), which is commentary with no new plot action — ending on Rusty's remorse is a correct stop, not a shortened one. So the census was right to mark both PT003 bands RESOLVES on the ending.

WHY THE TWO PT003 BANDS DIFFER: PT003 4-9 gets the Lively-sank sequence right — driver says "Lively is sick" (line 12), then "the men with him lied" (line 18) — matching source lines 806/810. PT003 9+ collapses the two reports onto the driver and is the one that slips (finding 1 below).

Clean (not listed): PT002 4-9 and PT003 4-9.
